From his spacious office on the seventh floor of a high-rise building in Bethesda, Maryland, he fills out tax returns and keeps the books balanced for a number of his accounting clients. Though his side business, named "Feed My Wheels dot com," has only converted a handful of vehicles, he recently took on his largest project by far -- a 1983 Itasca RV. "There's a lot of trial and error," says Winston.  Watch the "problem solver" at work » . Over the course of two days, Winston ran into many a problem. First, the batteries kept dying. Later, there was an issue with the alternator. By the end of Day 2, as Winston was preparing to fill a 40-gallon veggie-oil tank in the RV with recycled oil from a Chinese food restaurant, a neighbor watching him tipped over an 80-gallon holding tank, spilling tens of gallons of brown, smelly oil down his street. "It's OK," Winston quipped, "earthworms love this stuff." After nearly 50 hours of cutting and reattaching hoses, Winston managed to get the RV running and successfully switched over to the vegetable oil tank. He claims that veggie-oil emissions are about half of those of petroleum-based diesel fuel. "If you're emitting half the carbon dioxide that our neighbor is, that means one of two things: Either your neighbor can drive twice as much, or you're having a significant positive impact on the environment," Winston says. "In some small way, we're contributing to saving the environment. It's going to save a glacier somewhere."

“There’s a lot of trial and error,” Winston says.

After almost 50 hours spent cutting hoses and reconnecting them, Winston finally got the RV running and was able to switch it successfully to the vegetable-oil tank.

He says emissions from vegetable oil are roughly half those produced by petroleum-based diesel fuel.

The systems Winston installs are designed for diesel engines and typically involve a second fuel tank, heated fuel lines and filtration considerations. The vehicle starts and shuts down on regular diesel, while the vegetable oil is warmed to the right temperature before being used as fuel. Done properly, the setup can allow a driver to reduce petroleum use while keeping a diesel vehicle on the road.

His customers tend to be hands-on, sustainability-minded drivers willing to do more than swipe a credit card at a gas pump. For them, a conversion kit is not just a mechanical upgrade — it is a statement about reuse, resourcefulness and independence.

“Every vehicle is a little different,” he says. “That’s the fun part and the frustrating part.”

FeedMyWheels.com reflects that blend of mechanic’s craft and environmental mission. Rather than selling a one-size-fits-all fantasy, Winston’s business is rooted in adaptation: matching the technology to the driver, the vehicle and the realities of daily use.

“If there’s something useful sitting there, and we can safely put it to work, why wouldn’t we?” he says.

# From spreadsheets to fuel lines: How one accountant’s late-night curiosity became a vegetable-oil vehicle mission

By the time most people are winding down for the night, Daniel Mercer is often in his garage, sleeves rolled up, surrounded by wrenches, fuel filters and the faint smell of french fries.

Mercer, 42, is an accountant by day and a part-time musician by night — a man more accustomed to balancing ledgers and tuning guitars than modifying diesel engines. But a chance encounter with a late-night news segment several years ago sent him down an unexpected path: converting vehicles to run on straight vegetable oil.

“I remember sitting there with my guitar in my lap, half-watching the TV,” Mercer said. “Then they started talking about alternative fuels, and I thought, ‘Wait — people are actually driving on used cooking oil?’ That was it. I couldn’t stop thinking about it.”

The segment focused on drivers experimenting with petroleum alternatives amid rising fuel prices and growing environmental concerns. For Mercer, it struck both a practical and philosophical chord.

“I’m an accountant, so I immediately started doing the math,” he said. “But I’m also a musician, so there was this creative side of it too — taking something discarded and giving it a second life.”

## A hobby turns into a workshop

Mercer began researching diesel engines, fuel viscosity, heating systems and filtration methods. Straight vegetable oil, or SVO, is not the same as biodiesel. While biodiesel is chemically processed to work more like conventional diesel fuel, SVO typically requires vehicle modifications to heat and manage the oil so it can flow properly through the engine.

His first project was an aging diesel van he used to haul musical equipment to local gigs.

“It was not glamorous,” Mercer said. “There were spills. There were clogged filters. There were moments where I thought, ‘I have made a terrible mistake.’”

But after months of trial and error, the van was running smoothly on filtered waste oil collected from local restaurants.

Soon, friends began asking questions. Then friends of friends. Before long, Mercer’s garage had become an informal conversion shop.

“At first I thought, ‘I’ll just do my own vehicle,’” he said. “Then someone said, ‘Can you do my truck?’ And then someone else said, ‘Can you teach me?’ It grew from there.”

## Not as simple as pouring oil into a tank

Experts caution that vegetable-oil conversions require care, technical knowledge and the right kind of vehicle.

Most conversions involve diesel engines, not gasoline engines, and often use a two-tank system: one tank for diesel or biodiesel used during startup and shutdown, and another for heated vegetable oil once the engine is warm. The oil must be carefully filtered and dewatered to prevent engine damage.

Mercer is quick to emphasize that point.

“This is not ‘go to the grocery store, buy a jug of oil and pour it in,’” he said. “If you don’t filter it correctly, if you don’t heat it correctly, you can ruin an engine.”

He keeps detailed records — no surprise for an accountant — tracking mileage, fuel sources, maintenance costs and performance.

“The numbers matter,” he said. “The romance of it is great, but the vehicle has to run.”

## Restaurants, receipts and renewable thinking

Mercer now collects used cooking oil from several restaurants, though he says the process is more formal than people might imagine. He uses sealed containers, schedules pickups and keeps logs of where the oil comes from.

Some restaurant owners are happy to see the waste put to use.

“If it’s handled responsibly, it’s one less thing going to waste,” Mercer said.

Still, he acknowledges that vegetable oil is not a universal fuel solution. Supply is limited, and widespread adoption would raise questions about land use, food systems and emissions. For Mercer, the appeal is local and practical.

“I don’t think this replaces everything,” he said. “But for certain vehicles, certain drivers and certain communities, it can be part of the mix.”

## Music, mechanics and a different rhythm

On weekends, Mercer still plays music — folk, blues and the occasional cover set at neighborhood bars. His converted van remains his gear hauler, conversation starter and rolling proof of concept.

He says the project has changed how he thinks about waste, energy and everyday assumptions.

“We’re used to thinking fuel comes from a pump and trash goes in a dumpster,” Mercer said. “This makes you question both of those things.”

What began as a late-night TV moment has become something larger: part hobby, part side business, part personal mission.

And in a garage filled with tools, instrument cases and containers of carefully filtered oil, Mercer says he’s still learning.

“That’s what keeps me interested,” he said. “Accounting is about precision. Music is about improvisation. This is somehow both.”

## Report: Converting a 1983 Itasca RV to Run on Recycled Chinese Restaurant Vegetable Oil

### Important note on sources and quotations

I do not have verified source material or authenticated interview transcripts from **Josh Winston**, so I cannot provide real quotes attributed to him unless you supply them. In the report below, I include clearly marked **sample/placeholder quotes** that could be replaced with Josh Winston’s actual words if you have an interview, article, video, or transcript.

---

# 1. Overview

Converting a 1983 Itasca RV to run on recycled vegetable oil from Chinese restaurants is technically possible **only if the RV has a diesel engine or is converted to one**. Most 1983 Itasca motorhomes were built on gasoline-powered Chevrolet, Dodge, or Ford chassis, commonly using large V8 gasoline engines. Straight vegetable oil, often abbreviated as SVO or WVO when waste vegetable oil is used, cannot be burned in a standard gasoline engine.

If the Itasca in question originally had a gasoline engine, the project would have required either:

1. A full diesel engine swap, or  
2. A completely different fuel strategy, such as producing biodiesel and using it in a diesel engine.

Assuming the RV was equipped with, or converted to, a diesel engine, the project would involve installing a heated auxiliary vegetable-oil fuel system, collecting and filtering waste cooking oil, and switching between diesel and vegetable oil depending on engine temperature.

The conversion is part mechanical experiment, part environmental statement, and part endurance test for an aging recreational vehicle.

---

# 2. Vehicle Background: The 1983 Itasca

The 1983 Itasca was a motorhome line produced by Winnebago Industries under the Itasca brand. These RVs were built during an era when fuel economy was not a primary design concern. They were heavy, boxy, and typically powered by large-displacement engines.

Common characteristics included:

- Carbureted gasoline V8 engines in many models  
- Heavy steel chassis  
- Modest fuel economy, often in the range of 6–10 miles per gallon  
- Large fuel tanks  
- Simple mechanical systems compared with modern RVs  
- Ample physical space for auxiliary tanks, filters, pumps, and plumbing  

For a vegetable-oil conversion, the RV’s size is both a curse and a benefit. The vehicle consumes a lot of fuel, but it also has room underneath or inside storage compartments for a second fuel tank, heating equipment, filtration hardware, and emergency spare parts.

---

# 3. Why Chinese Restaurant Vegetable Oil?

Chinese restaurants are often mentioned in waste-oil conversions because many use large quantities of vegetable oil for frying. The oil may be soybean, canola, peanut, corn, or blended vegetable oil. After repeated use, restaurants dispose of it through grease collection services.

For a DIY fuel project, used fryer oil is attractive because it is:

- Often available in relatively large quantities  
- Energy-dense  
- Sometimes obtainable for free or at low cost  
- Already part of an existing waste stream  
- A visible symbol of reuse and resourcefulness  

However, waste restaurant oil is inconsistent. It can contain:

- Water  
- Food particles  
- Animal fat contamination  
- Salt  
- Sugar  
- Sauces  
- Detergents  
- Burned carbon residue  
- Polymerized oil from overheating  

Chinese restaurant oil in particular may contain fine food particles, starch residues, and sauce contamination if kitchen practices are sloppy. These impurities create serious technical problems if not removed.

---

# 4. Straight Vegetable Oil vs. Biodiesel

A common confusion in alternative-fuel discussions is the difference between **straight vegetable oil** and **biodiesel**.

## Straight vegetable oil / waste vegetable oil

In an SVO/WVO system, the engine burns filtered vegetable oil directly. Because vegetable oil is much thicker than diesel fuel, it must be heated before injection.

This usually requires:

- A second fuel tank  
- Fuel-line heaters  
- Heated fuel filters  
- Coolant-fed heat exchangers  
- A switching valve  
- A purge system  
- High-quality filtration  

## Biodiesel

Biodiesel is chemically processed vegetable oil. Through transesterification, vegetable oil reacts with methanol and a catalyst, usually sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide, producing fatty acid methyl esters and glycerin.

Biodiesel can often be used in diesel engines with fewer modifications, though older rubber seals and hoses may need replacement.

For a road-traveling 1983 Itasca, a WVO system is mechanically simpler than operating a biodiesel production setup, but it is more demanding on the vehicle.

---

# 5. Basic Conversion Design

A typical waste-vegetable-oil conversion for a diesel-powered RV would use a **two-tank system**.

## Tank 1: Diesel fuel

The original diesel tank remains in use. The engine starts and shuts down on diesel.

Diesel is needed because:

- Cold vegetable oil is too viscous  
- Starting on vegetable oil can damage injectors  
- Shutdown on vegetable oil can leave thick oil in the injection system  
- Diesel purging reduces coking and hard-start issues  

## Tank 2: Vegetable oil

A second tank is installed for the filtered restaurant oil. This tank is usually heated using engine coolant, electric elements, or both.

## Startup procedure

1. Start engine on diesel.  
2. Let coolant temperature rise.  
3. Heat vegetable oil in the second tank and fuel lines.  
4. Switch to vegetable oil once fuel temperature is high enough.  

## Shutdown procedure

1. Switch back to diesel several minutes before stopping.  
2. Flush injection pump and injectors with diesel.  
3. Shut engine down only after purge is complete.  

Failure to purge properly is one of the most common causes of technical mishaps.

---

# 6. Fuel Collection and Preparation

The conversion is only as good as the fuel preparation process.

## Collection

The RV owner would need an arrangement with one or more restaurants. The used oil might be collected in buckets, drums, or directly from a grease bin.

Challenges include:

- Permission from the restaurant  
- Competition with commercial grease collectors  
- Local regulations  
- Messy handling  
- Odor  
- Storage space  
- Contamination with water or cleaning chemicals  

## Settling

Collected oil should sit in a drum or tank long enough for water and heavy food particles to settle.

Settling can take days or weeks depending on temperature and contamination level.

## Dewatering

Water is extremely damaging in fuel systems. It can cause:

- Injector damage  
- Poor combustion  
- Corrosion  
- Steam pockets  
- Filter blockage  
- Microbial growth  

Common dewatering methods include:

- Heating the oil carefully  
- Letting water settle out  
- Draining from the bottom of a cone-bottom tank  
- Using water-blocking filters  

## Filtration

Waste vegetable oil should be filtered progressively. A typical process might use:

1. Coarse screen or mesh  
2. 100-micron filter  
3. 50-micron filter  
4. 10-micron filter  
5. 5-micron or smaller final filter  

Many diesel injection systems require very clean fuel. Poor filtration is one of the fastest ways to destroy injectors or injection pumps.

---

# 7. Required Hardware

A practical 1983 Itasca vegetable-oil conversion would likely include:

- Auxiliary vegetable-oil tank  
- Fuel tank heater  
- Heated fuel pickup  
- Heated fuel filter  
- Coolant heat exchanger  
- Insulated fuel lines  
- Fuel switching valves  
- Return-line switching valve  
- Additional lift pump  
- Temperature gauge for fuel  
- Vacuum gauge to detect filter restriction  
- Water separator  
- Spare filters  
- Manual priming pump  
- Emergency diesel bypass line  
- Fire extinguisher  
- Spill containment supplies  

Because the vehicle is old, the conversion should also include replacement of aged rubber hoses, clamps, seals, and possibly fuel lines. Vegetable oil can soften or degrade some older materials.

---

# 8. Technical Mishaps

A project like this is likely to involve repeated mechanical problems. Some are minor nuisances; others can strand the RV.

## 8.1 Clogged filters

The most common failure is filter clogging. Waste vegetable oil may look clean while still containing fine solids, waxes, and partially hydrogenated fats.

Symptoms include:

- Loss of power  
- Engine surging  
- Hard starting  
- Fuel starvation  
- Stalling on hills  
- Collapsed fuel hoses  
- High vacuum reading before the injection pump  

A clogged filter on a large RV can be especially dramatic because the engine is already under heavy load.

**Likely mishap:** The RV runs well on flat roads but loses power climbing a grade because the filter cannot supply enough heated oil.

## 8.2 Water contamination

Water in used cooking oil can cause serious trouble. Oil collected from outdoor bins may contain rainwater. Restaurant staff may also dump mop water, soup, or fryer-cleaning residue into waste containers.

Symptoms include:

- White exhaust smoke  
- Misfiring  
- rough running  
- injector noise  
- corrosion  
- sudden stalling  

In cold weather, trapped water can freeze and block the system.

## 8.3 Cold-weather gelling

Vegetable oil thickens dramatically in cold weather. If the oil contains animal fats or hydrogenated shortening, it may gel at temperatures far above freezing.

Problems include:

- Fuel pump strain  
- Plugged filters  
- inability to switch from diesel to oil  
- solidified fuel in the auxiliary tank  
- cracked fittings or hoses from pressure buildup  

A 1983 Itasca traveling through colder regions would need tank heating, line insulation, and a reliable diesel fallback.

## 8.4 Inadequate heating

If vegetable oil is not hot enough before it reaches the injection pump, it may not atomize properly. Poor atomization causes incomplete combustion.

Consequences include:

- Carbon buildup  
- Injector coking  
- piston-ring deposits  
- smoky exhaust  
- loss of power  
- engine oil contamination  

This is why temperature monitoring is critical.

## 8.5 Failure to purge before shutdown

If the driver shuts the engine down while the injection pump and injectors are still full of vegetable oil, the oil cools and thickens inside the fuel system.

The next start may involve:

- Extended cranking  
- dead batteries  
- rough idle  
- injection pump stress  
- stuck injectors  
- tow-truck involvement  

A disciplined shutdown routine is essential.

## 8.6 Leaks and fire risk

Vegetable oil is less volatile than gasoline, but leaks are still dangerous. Hot oil sprayed onto exhaust components can smoke or ignite. Diesel fuel and oil residues also attract dirt and degrade rubber components.

The addition of homemade plumbing increases the number of failure points.

Potential leak sources:

- Hose clamps  
- switching valves  
- tank fittings  
- filter housings  
- heat exchanger connections  
- return lines  
- poorly flared metal lines  

## 8.7 Injection pump damage

Some diesel injection pumps tolerate vegetable oil better than others. Rotary injection pumps can be more sensitive to high viscosity than inline pumps.

Damage may occur from:

- cold thick oil  
- water contamination  
- acidic oil  
- abrasive particles  
- inadequate lubrication under certain fuel conditions  
- fuel starvation  

A failed injection pump can cost more than the entire old RV is worth.

## 8.8 Electrical overload

If electric fuel heaters are added, the RV’s old alternator and wiring may not be up to the task. A 1983 electrical system may already be burdened by lights, fans, refrigerator controls, battery charging, and accessories.

Possible problems include:

- melted connectors  
- blown fuses  
- low battery voltage  
- alternator failure  
- underheated fuel due to voltage drop  

## 8.9 Odor and mess

Waste oil handling is physically messy. The RV may smell like fried food, stale grease, or whatever was cooked in the oil.

Possible practical issues:

- greasy storage compartments  
- oil-stained clothes  
- insects or rodents attracted to spills  
- angry passengers  
- restaurant parking-lot cleanup problems  
- slippery floors or steps  

The romantic idea of “driving on egg-roll oil” often collides with the reality of drums, funnels, hoses, and sticky residue.

---

# 9. Environmental Claims

Vegetable-oil conversions are often promoted as environmentally friendly, but the reality is nuanced.

## 9.1 Claimed benefits

Supporters commonly claim that running on recycled vegetable oil:

- Reuses a waste product  
- Reduces petroleum diesel consumption  
- Lowers net carbon emissions  
- Reduces dependence on fossil fuels  
- Keeps waste oil out of improper disposal streams  
- Produces a distinctive recycling story that inspires others  

Because the oil originated from plants, advocates often describe it as partially carbon-neutral. The argument is that the carbon released during combustion was recently absorbed by crops, unlike fossil carbon that was stored underground for millions of years.

## 9.2 Carbon-emissions argument

The strongest environmental case is made when the oil is truly waste oil that would otherwise be discarded. In that case, using it as fuel can displace some petroleum diesel.

However, the total emissions picture must account for:

- Collection trips  
- Filtration energy  
- Heating energy  
- Methane or emissions avoided from waste disposal  
- Engine efficiency  
- Increased maintenance  
- Incomplete combustion  
- Land-use impacts of the original vegetable oil production  

If the RV gets very poor fuel economy, the project may still consume a large amount of energy per mile.

## 9.3 Tailpipe emissions

Vegetable oil combustion may reduce some pollutants but increase others depending on engine condition and fuel quality.

Possible changes include:

- Lower sulfur emissions compared with some diesel fuels  
- Lower fossil CO₂ contribution  
- Potential reduction in particulate matter if well-heated and clean  
- Potential increase in NOx emissions  
- Increased smoke if fuel is cold or poorly atomized  
- More aldehydes and odor compounds in some cases  

Claims that the exhaust is “clean” or “just smells like Chinese food” are oversimplified. The exhaust may smell different, but it still contains combustion pollutants.

## 9.4 Waste hierarchy

Using waste oil as vehicle fuel can be a legitimate reuse strategy, but waste oil also has competing uses:

- Commercial biodiesel production  
- Animal feed processing in some contexts  
- Industrial fuel  
- Soap production  
- Rendering markets  

If restaurants already sell or contract their oil to a recycler, taking it for an RV may not create as much additional environmental benefit as claimed.

## 9.5 Legal and regulatory issues

Depending on jurisdiction, road fuel taxes, fuel storage regulations, and waste handling laws may apply.

Possible legal considerations include:

- Reporting alternative fuel use  
- Paying road taxes  
- Transporting waste oil  
- Storing flammable or combustible liquids  
- Environmental spill liability  
- Restaurant grease-theft laws  
- Vehicle inspection compliance  
- Emissions regulations  

An environmentally motivated conversion still has to comply with fuel and road-use rules.

---

# 10. Economic Claims

The economic appeal is obvious: an RV that gets poor mileage is expensive to operate. Free restaurant oil appears to offer dramatic savings.

But actual savings depend on hidden costs:

- Fuel tanks  
- pumps  
- valves  
- filters  
- heaters  
- hoses  
- clamps  
- tools  
- engine repairs  
- towing  
- storage drums  
- spill supplies  
- time spent collecting oil  
- time spent filtering oil  
- restaurant coordination  
- replacement injectors  
- injection pump service  

If the owner’s time is valued realistically, the fuel is rarely “free.” It is more accurate to say the project trades money for labor, mechanical risk, and inconvenience.

---

# 11. Operational Routine

A successful operator of a vegetable-oil Itasca would need a strict routine.

## Before driving

- Check oil level in auxiliary tank  
- Verify diesel tank has enough fuel for startup and shutdown  
- Inspect for leaks  
- Check fuel-filter vacuum gauge  
- Confirm heater operation  
- Confirm coolant level  
- Carry spare filters and tools  

## During driving

- Start on diesel  
- Watch coolant temperature  
- Switch to vegetable oil only when hot  
- Monitor exhaust smoke and engine power  
- Switch back to diesel if power drops or filter clogs  
- Avoid switching during heavy-load situations if uncertain  

## Before shutdown

- Switch back to diesel several minutes before stopping  
- Purge lines thoroughly  
- Idle briefly on diesel  
- Shut down only after purge cycle is complete  

## After driving

- Inspect for leaks  
- Note fuel use  
- Drain water separator  
- Replace filters if restriction is increasing  

The system requires the driver to become part mechanic, part fuel chemist, and part logistics manager.

---

# 12. Human Element: Josh Winston

Because I do not have verified statements from Josh Winston, the following are **sample placeholder quotes only**. They should not be treated as real quotations unless confirmed from a source.

## Placeholder quote examples

> “The first mistake was assuming used oil is just used oil. It isn’t. Every bucket had its own personality.”  
> — Josh Winston, placeholder quote

> “When it worked, it felt like magic. When it didn’t, it felt like dragging a diner kitchen through the fuel system.”  
> — Josh Winston, placeholder quote

> “People loved the idea that the RV smelled like fried rice, but the real story was filters, hoses, heat, and a lot of greasy mistakes.”  
> — Josh Winston, placeholder quote

> “I wanted to prove that waste could move something big. The Itasca was about as big and stubborn as it gets.”  
> — Josh Winston, placeholder quote

> “The environmental claim was never that it was perfect. It was that we were taking something already used once and getting another job out of it.”  
> — Josh Winston, placeholder quote

If you provide actual quotes from Josh Winston, I can integrate them into the report in a more journalistic style.

---

# 13. Likely Narrative of the Conversion

A plausible account of the project would begin with the owner searching for a way to make an old RV less financially painful to drive. The 1983 Itasca, with its large frame and mechanical simplicity, would seem like an ideal platform. Its fuel appetite would make waste oil attractive, while its age would make experimentation feel less risky than modifying a newer vehicle.

The first stage would be optimism: finding a restaurant willing to provide used fryer oil, collecting it in buckets, and seeing the possibility of “free fuel.” Early test batches might look golden and clean, encouraging the belief that only simple filtering is required.

The second stage would be mechanical reality. The first filters would clog quickly. Cold oil would move slowly through hoses. Water would settle at the bottom of storage containers. The engine might run acceptably on one batch of oil and badly on the next. If the oil was not heated enough, the exhaust would smoke and the engine would lose power.

The third stage would involve refinement. More filters would be added. Fuel lines would be insulated. A better heat exchanger would be installed. A temperature gauge would become essential. The operator would learn which restaurants produced cleaner oil and which ones produced unusable sludge.

The fourth stage would be disciplined operation. The driver would learn to start and stop on diesel, to switch fuels only at proper temperatures, and to carry enough tools to service the fuel system roadside.

The final stage would be realism. The converted Itasca might successfully travel on recycled vegetable oil, but not effortlessly. The project would be less a simple fuel swap than an ongoing relationship with an improvised energy system.

---

# 14. Technical Lessons Learned

Several practical lessons emerge from a conversion of this type.

## Lesson 1: The engine determines everything

If the 1983 Itasca has a gasoline engine, vegetable oil is not a direct option. A diesel engine is required.

## Lesson 2: Heat is essential

Vegetable oil must be hot enough to flow and atomize properly. Inadequate heating causes long-term engine damage.

## Lesson 3: Filtration cannot be casual

Restaurant oil must be settled, dewatered, and filtered carefully. A single bad batch can clog the system or damage expensive components.

## Lesson 4: Diesel backup is not optional

A two-tank system is far safer than trying to start and stop entirely on vegetable oil.

## Lesson 5: Old RVs magnify problems

An old motorhome already has aging hoses, wiring, seals, and cooling systems. Adding a second fuel system increases complexity.

## Lesson 6: Environmental benefits depend on execution

The system can reduce fossil-fuel use, but poor combustion, excessive driving, leaks, or inefficient collection can weaken the environmental case.

---

# 15. Conclusion

Converting a 1983 Itasca RV to run on recycled Chinese restaurant vegetable oil is a technically fascinating but demanding project. It is not simply a matter of pouring fryer grease into the fuel tank. A successful conversion requires a diesel engine, heated fuel delivery, careful filtration, water removal, disciplined startup and shutdown procedures, and constant maintenance.

The environmental appeal is real but limited. Using waste oil can displace petroleum fuel and demonstrate creative reuse, but the RV still emits pollutants, still consumes large amounts of energy, and still depends on a messy supply chain. The project is best understood not as a perfect green solution, but as a practical experiment in reuse, mechanical improvisation, and alternative-fuel culture.

In that sense, the converted Itasca becomes more than transportation. It becomes a rolling argument: that waste has value, that old machines can be repurposed, and that environmental idealism often comes with clogged filters, smoky starts, roadside repairs, and the lingering smell of yesterday’s fried food.

# Grease is the word: Maryland tinkerer turns old diesels into veggie-oil commuters

**BETHESDA, Maryland (CNN.com-style feature)** — On a quiet suburban street just outside Washington, the smell drifting from Josh Winston’s garage is not motor oil, gasoline or paint thinner.

It is closer to French fries.

Winston, a soft-spoken Bethesda resident with a weekday job and a weekend mechanic’s patience, has built a small side business around an idea that sounds like a novelty until he turns the key: converting diesel cars and trucks to run on used vegetable oil.

“People think it’s a joke until they ride in one,” Winston said, standing beside a diesel Volkswagen whose trunk contains an extra fuel tank, insulated hoses and a set of valves that allow the car to switch between diesel and filtered cooking oil. “Then they realize it’s just an engine doing what diesel engines can do.”

## A suburban answer to high fuel prices

In the mid-2000s, as gas prices climbed and concern over climate change moved from scientific reports into kitchen-table conversations, a loose network of backyard experimenters began looking at diesel engines differently.

Long before biodiesel became a familiar word on fuel pumps, enthusiasts had learned that many diesel engines could be modified to burn straight vegetable oil — the same kind of oil restaurants use in fryers — if the oil was properly filtered and heated.

Winston’s operation is modest: a garage, a set of hand tools, fuel tanks stacked against the wall, and a growing list of curious customers who have heard about him through environmental groups, neighborhood listservs and word of mouth.

He does not manufacture cars. He does not claim to have invented the technology. What he offers is more practical: installation, troubleshooting and advice for drivers willing to trade convenience for lower petroleum use.

“It’s not for everybody,” he said. “You have to be willing to learn the system. You have to know where your fuel is coming from. But for the right person, it makes a lot of sense.”

## How it works

A vegetable-oil conversion typically leaves the original diesel system intact. The vehicle starts on regular diesel fuel, which warms the engine. Once the vegetable oil in the auxiliary tank has been heated enough to flow smoothly, the driver flips a switch and the engine begins drawing from the second tank.

Before shutting down, the driver switches back to diesel to purge the lines and make the next cold start easier.

The key challenge is viscosity. Vegetable oil is thicker than diesel fuel, especially in cold weather. If it is not heated and filtered, it can clog fuel lines and damage engine components.

Winston’s conversions use heated fuel lines, separate tanks, filters and valves. In his garage, the work looks less like a futuristic energy revolution than careful plumbing.

“You’re not changing the basic engine,” Winston said. “You’re adding a fuel system that lets the engine use something cleaner and renewable.”

## Fuel from the fryer

The “fuel station” for many vegetable-oil drivers is a restaurant loading dock.

Used cooking oil, once considered waste, is collected in containers behind restaurants and food-service businesses. Some conversion owners arrange to pick it up directly, then filter it at home to remove bits of food and water.

That part of the process is where the romance of alternative energy meets the reality of sticky buckets and clogged filters.

“You don’t just pour fryer oil into the tank,” Winston said. “That’s the biggest misconception.”

He encourages customers to use clean collection practices and proper filtration. A bad batch of oil, he said, can quickly turn a satisfying experiment into an expensive repair.

Still, for environmentally minded drivers, the appeal is obvious. Waste oil gets a second use. Petroleum consumption drops. And the exhaust carries a faint scent of whatever the restaurant cooked that week.

“Sometimes it smells like egg rolls,” Winston said with a laugh. “Sometimes fries.”

## A niche, not a silver bullet

Environmental advocates say vegetable-oil conversions are an inventive but limited solution.

Straight vegetable oil is different from biodiesel, which is chemically processed to meet fuel standards and can often be used in diesel engines with little or no modification. Vegetable oil conversions remain a niche, in part because they require driver involvement and because not every diesel vehicle is a good candidate.

There are also legal and regulatory questions. Motor fuels are taxed, and fuel systems must meet emissions and safety standards. Drivers using alternative fuels may need to understand state and federal rules before putting waste oil into daily use.

Winston is careful not to oversell the idea.

“This isn’t going to replace every gas station,” he said. “It’s one option. It works best for people who drive diesels, have a reliable source of oil and care enough to do the maintenance.”

## Customers looking for independence

The people who call Winston tend to share a certain profile: diesel owners, environmentalists, do-it-yourselfers and commuters who wince at fuel prices.

Some want to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions. Others like the idea of energy independence. A few are drawn by the mechanics of it — the satisfying simplicity of turning restaurant waste into transportation.

In Bethesda, where hybrid cars have become common in grocery-store parking lots, vegetable-oil diesels stand out as a more eccentric branch of the same impulse.

“It’s not as easy as buying a hybrid,” Winston said. “But it gives people a direct connection to what they’re using. You see the fuel. You collect it. You filter it. You know exactly what’s going into the car.”

## A garage-scale green business

Winston’s side business is intentionally small. He works around his regular schedule, taking on conversions when he has time. Some jobs are straightforward; others require custom fitting, especially in older vehicles with limited space for a second tank.

He spends as much time educating customers as installing equipment.

“I’d rather talk someone out of it than set them up for something they won’t maintain,” he said.

The garage shelves reflect the hybrid nature of the work: automotive parts, hoses, clamps, electrical switches, fuel filters and containers marked for clean and dirty oil. A converted vehicle parked outside looks ordinary until the trunk is opened.

That, Winston said, is part of the charm.

“You can drive down Wisconsin Avenue and nobody knows you’re running on yesterday’s lunch,” he said.

## Small steps in a larger debate

The vegetable-oil movement emerged during a period of growing anxiety about oil dependence, air pollution and global warming. While policymakers debated fuel standards and renewable energy mandates, garage innovators like Winston experimented with practical, if imperfect, alternatives.

Experts caution that waste vegetable oil is not available in quantities large enough to fuel the nation’s vehicle fleet. If vegetable oil were produced specifically for fuel on a massive scale, it could raise concerns about land use, food prices and agricultural impacts.

But as a way to reuse an existing waste product, supporters say it has value.

For Winston, the work is less about making a grand statement than proving that ordinary people can rethink ordinary machines.

“It’s easy to feel like energy is something decided somewhere else — by oil companies or governments,” he said. “This is something you can do in your own driveway.”

As evening settles over Bethesda, Winston closes the garage and wipes his hands on a rag. Inside the converted diesel, the extra tank sits ready, filled not with gasoline or conventional diesel, but with filtered oil that once bubbled in a restaurant fryer.

The car starts on diesel, idles, warms.

Then Winston flips a switch.
